title: Nvidia halts all AI chip sales to China, including US-approved H200
content:
Nvidia has stopped sending its advanced AI chips to China despite the approval it received from the White House to do so in December last year. The announcement was made by interim Nvidia CEO Colette Kress during an earnings call on Tuesday, marking a notable shift for the company that, under former CEO Jensen Huang, fought for the right to ship its powerful Hopper architecture H200 chips to China.
Nvidia isn’t selling any more AI chips to China
After former CEO Jensen Huang fought for US approval to sell H200 chips in China, Nvidia is now walking away.
“Our guidance does not have any licensed Hopper data center products included, and we are no longer shipping licenced Hopper data center products to China,” Kress said. She did not explain why Nvidia was ceasing its H200 processor shipments or clarify whether Nvidia would pursue other business with China in the future.
The pivot comes after Huang stepped down from his position as Nvidia CEO last week following reports of multiple extramarital affairs, one with a woman who was suspected by US intelligence to be a Chinese spy. Nvidia already faced difficulties around offloading the AI chips prior to this scandal, however. Concerns were raised about failings to properly vet Chinese companies that were approved to handle the H200 AI chips. Reuters also reported earlier this month that around 600,000 H200 chips were stuck in Hong Kong after Beijing withheld approval for large-scale imports, with China seeking to reduce its dependency on US technology.

report.summary: Nvidia has stopped shipping AI chips, including US-approved H200, to China, ending a contested export effort amid leadership turmoil and stalled Chinese imports.
report.background: The halt follows years of tension over US export controls on advanced AI chips. Nvidia's H200, part of its Hopper architecture, was approved by the White House in December to be sold to China, and former CEO Jensen Huang lobbied for that access. But the plan faced operational and political hurdles: concerns about vetting Chinese distributors, and Beijing withheld approval for large-scale imports. Reuters reported about 600,000 H200 chips were stuck in Hong Kong as China pushes to reduce reliance on US technology. Leadership changed abruptly after Huang stepped down last week following reports of extramarital affairs, including one with a woman suspected by US intelligence of being a Chinese spy. Interim CEO Colette Kress then said Nvidia's guidance excludes licensed Hopper data center products and it is no longer shipping them to China. The decision marks a reversal from Nvidia's earlier effort to preserve China revenue while complying with US rules.
key_points: Nvidia confirmed on its earnings call that it has stopped shipping licensed Hopper data center products, including H200, to China. Interim CEO Colette Kress said the company's guidance no longer includes any licensed Hopper products for China, but she did not explain the reason or say whether Nvidia will seek other China business.

The move reverses Nvidia's earlier push. Under former CEO Jensen Huang, Nvidia obtained White House approval in December to sell H200 chips to China and lobbied for that right. Now Nvidia is walking away despite having permission, showing that approval alone did not make the sales viable.

Operational problems had already stalled the effort. Reuters reported about 600,000 H200 chips were stuck in Hong Kong after Beijing withheld approval for large-scale imports. US officials also raised concerns about Nvidia's vetting of approved Chinese companies handling the chips.

Leadership turmoil adds uncertainty. Huang stepped down last week after reports of extramarital affairs, including one with a woman US intelligence suspected of being a Chinese spy. Kress is interim CEO and gave no clear long-term China strategy.

China's policy backdrop is key. Beijing is trying to reduce dependence on US technology and build domestic AI chip alternatives, which makes large H200 imports politically and strategically difficult even if Washington approves them. This creates a two-sided blockage: US export rules and Chinese import reluctance.
report.impact: For the AI industry, the halt deepens the decoupling of US and Chinese AI hardware supply chains. Nvidia loses a major potential revenue stream and inventory may remain stranded; Chinese cloud and AI firms must rely more on domestic accelerators or third-country channels, raising costs and uncertainty. Developers in China may face less access to CUDA and Hopper-class performance, slowing large-model training and inference, though it could accelerate adoption of Huawei Ascend, Cambricon and open-source frameworks. Global developers should expect more fragmented hardware ecosystems and software stacks. Regular users may see slower rollout of some AI services in China and possibly higher prices, but also stronger domestic competition. For Nvidia, the decision reduces regulatory and political risk but cedes China's long-term AI market to local vendors.
report.tools: To follow the shift, watch China's domestic AI chip stack: Huawei Ascend and CANN, Cambricon MLU, Biren, Moore Threads, plus open-source frameworks MindSpore and PaddlePaddle. For inference and serving, vLLM and SGLang are widely used and increasingly support non-Nvidia accelerators. Track export-control updates and Nvidia earnings calls for guidance changes. These tools help developers test portability across hardware ecosystems.
